fixes.explanation: Pharaoh asks, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?” That's the king of Egypt putting it to his officials out loud. They had just been pleased with the proposal (v. 37). When a king says that about you, your résumé is done.

Nobody in this scene draws a sword, friend. Joseph explained Pharaoh's dreams and suggested a plan for the food (Genesis 41:25-36). Pharaoh's question after that is about the Spirit of God abiding in him, not about any soldier's heart.

Pharaoh says, “Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.” He puts Joseph over his house and tells all his people to obey Joseph's commands. The one place he stays above Joseph is the throne, the king's own place. A boss can hand off nearly everything and still keep the name on the door.
Pharaoh “…clothed him in garments of fine linen…” That comes right after the signet ring went onto Joseph's finger. A gold chain went around his neck too. That's a whole new look for a whole new job.

The text says Joseph rode in Pharaoh's second chariot, with men calling out before him, “Bow the knee!” Then it says Pharaoh placed him over all the land of Egypt. That's a loud way to start a new job.

Pharaoh does give Joseph something here, but it isn't a weapon. Along with the new name, he gives Joseph a wife named Asenath. Her father was Potiphera, a priest of On. A sword would have made for an odd wedding present.

Pharaoh doesn't hand Joseph any livestock in this scene. He gives him a wife, Asenath, whose father was Potiphera, a priest of On. The gift comes in the same verse as the new name, Zaphenath-paneah. Joseph walks away with a new name and a new family member.

The text says, “…Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt.” Thirty, and he's about to take charge of the whole land. After that, the verse says he left Pharaoh's presence and traveled throughout the land of Egypt. Some folks at thirty are still picking a phone plan.
The text says, “In every city he laid up the food from the fields around it.” So each city's stored food came from the fields around that city. That's a lot of storing. Joseph did it city by city.

Hills sound like a fair guess, but they aren't what the text says. Joseph “…laid up the food from the fields around it.” So the food came from the fields near each city. Hills may look pretty, but the fields are what the verse names.

You got it, because Joseph “…stopped keeping track of it…” The grain was “…like the sand of the sea…” and the text says “…it was beyond measure.” That's how much there was. Even the man doing the storing couldn't keep up with the count.

Joseph says, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.” That's the name he gives his firstborn, Manasseh. Joseph credits God, not himself. The hardship was real, and I think this name is how he talks about it.

Pharaoh was the one who had the dreams (Genesis 41:1-7), but the words about the years came from Joseph. Joseph told him seven years of abundance were coming, and then seven years of famine (Genesis 41:29-30). The text says the famine began “…just as Joseph had said.”

Pharaoh called for the magicians of Egypt, and no one could interpret his dreams for him (Genesis 41:8). The words about the years came from Joseph (Genesis 41:29-30). The text says the famine began “…just as Joseph had said.”

The people cried out to Pharaoh for food, and his answer was short. He told all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” Earlier in the passage, Pharaoh placed Joseph over all the land of Egypt (v. 41), and now the people hear it in plain words. That's a clear chain of command.

Waiting at home isn't what Pharaoh says. He tells all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” The people had cried out to him for food, and his answer sends them to Joseph. There's nothing in it about waiting for the famine to end.
You got it, baker. Joseph “…opened up all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians…” The text says sold, not gave. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt, and the grain went out as a sale.

The Ishmaelites show up earlier in Joseph's story, as the ones who bought him from his brothers (Genesis 37:28). But this passage doesn't name them at all. It says “…every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain…” That's wider than one group.
